cues.text: A Life Consecrated from Childhood
According to Pope St. Gregory the Great 's Dialogues — virtually the sole surviving source for her life — Scholastica was born around 480 at Nursia, in central Italy.
She belonged to the same noble family as her brother Benedict , later tradition holding the two to have been twins.
Gregory records simply that she had been 'dedicated from her infancy to Our Lord,' consecrating her life to God from childhood.
A Convent Near Monte Cassino
After Benedict established his renowned monastery at Monte Cassino, Scholastica settled nearby at Plombariola, some five miles distant.
There, she founded and governed a community of women, traditionally regarded as the foundress of Benedictine monasticism’s women’s branch.
Her sisters followed the same Rule her brother had written for his own monks.
The Annual Visit
Though unable, as an enclosed nun, to enter her brother's monastery, Scholastica met with Benedict once each year at a house near the abbey gate.

There, the two would spend the day together discussing spiritual matters — a practice of sibling devotion within a shared religious vocation that has become one of the most cherished images in the whole Benedictine tradition.
The Final Meeting and the Storm

Gregory the Great records their final meeting, when Scholastica, sensing it might be their last, begged Benedict to stay through the night so their conversation on 'the joys of the heavenly life' might continue.
When Benedict, bound by his monastic rule against remaining away from his cell overnight, insisted he must return, Scholastica bowed her head in prayer.
A sudden violent storm broke out, making it impossible for Benedict and his companions to leave.
Benedict, astonished, exclaimed, 'May Almighty God forgive you, sister; what have you done?'
to which Scholastica replied simply that she had asked a favor of God and He had granted it.
Death and Burial
Three days after this final meeting, Scholastica died at her convent.
Informed by a vision in which he saw his sister's soul ascend to heaven in the form of a dove, Benedict had her body brought to Monte Cassino.
He buried her in the tomb he had prepared for himself — so that in Gregory's words, death itself could not separate in body those whose minds had always been united in God.
Legacy
Scholastica is venerated as the foundress of Benedictine women's monasticism, a tradition that has flourished continuously for over fifteen centuries since her death.
Her story — of a request granted through prayer even against her brother's own rule — remains one of the most beloved illustrations in the Christian tradition.
It shows how holy love can, in Gregory's own words, accomplish more than strict observance alone.
